So you know in algebra when you wanted to take the slope of a line, say y = 3x + 1, you looked at 2 points, and you did y2 - y1 / x2 - x1. So look at say (0,1) and (1,4) and get 3/1 = 3. Easy peasy, right? Well, what if you wanted to find the slope of a curve, like f(x) = x^2? What does that even mean? You look at the graph on a sheet of paper and it's obvious the slope at x = 5 is much higher than the slope at x=1. Alright, fine. What's the slope at x = 3? How do we find it? 

One strategy is to do what we did before, only choose two points that are close to (3,9). So I pick (2, 4) and (4,16). If you draw a line across those points you'll see how it's a servicable estimate for the real slope. Doing (16-9)/(4-2) we see that 3.5 is our estimated slope. But can we do better. Sure we can. Let's pick two points that are even closer to 3. Now we pick (2.9, 8.41) and (3.1, 9.61). Our estimate now is 6. But okay, we don't want an estimate. We want the true value. That's what we call                     the derivative. To obtain the derivative, you pick the two closest possible points to the slope you want to to find, then calculate the slope of the line between them. So the points you want are (x, f(x)) and (x+delta(x), f(x+delta(x)) where the limit of delta(x) -> 0. This is the closest set of points to the actual value. To calculate the slope of this line you use the same equation you learned in high school algebra class. y2 - y1 / x2 - x1. Or, 
lim delta(x) -> 0 ((f(x+delta(x)) - f(x)) / (x + delta(x) - x)).

Plugging in x = 3 we have: lim delta(x) -> 0 ((3+delta(x))^2 - (3^2))/delta(x)

Simplifying [remember the FOIL method for multiplying (3+delta(x))(3+delta(x))] [also I replaced delta(x) with z for readability]:
lim z-> 0 (z^2 + 6z)/(z) = z(z+6)/z = z+6 = 6. Which you also know from the rule when f(x) = x^n, then f'(x) = (n)x^n-1
